about: Herio (Noirmoutier), Saint Philibert's island: one port, written 6 October 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/herio.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not attested. The dossier's cautions are kept: no raid of 799 is laid on this island, the salt beds on the island itself are supposed and not attested, no market, toll or mint is recorded here, and no lasting Northmen's base is claimed. Every named islander and the two monks Vitalis and Natalis are the game's.
woven: Woven with Quentovic, Rotomagus, Parisius, Namnetis and Burdigala on 6 Oct 2026: ties answered both ways; the people this file named in other ports are now real there (burdigala.oil_seller, quentovic.corbie_agent, namnetis.rainald); beats placed across the region and the port's cards (encounters/neustria_west_793.json) put on their sites. Nothing was taken out.

ports.summary: A low island south of the Loire mouth, two rocky islets joined by a sand bar and a lagoon, with Saint Philibert's monastery on the northern one and the founder's body in a marble coffin under three lamps. In 793 it lies under Louis, the king's son, king of Aquitaine; no toll is taken and no coin is struck, and what is sold is sold on the sand at Conca, where ships anchor to wait for a wind. A merchant comes for grey bay salt, cheapest of anything he will ever load, and brings what an island of monks cannot grow: grain, lamp oil, wine, lead, shoes and cloth.
ports.seasons: Salt is raked from midsummer until the autumn rains and is cheapest after the Assumption; the saint's feast is kept through the night before the twentieth day of August. The same fair weather that dries the salt brings the heathen ships, so from 819 the monks spend the sailing months at Deas on the mainland and the island is kept by a few brothers, the abbey's armed men and the islanders. The ebbs rule every day of it: the monastery's channel dries twice a day, and the flats west and south are bare rock and sand at low water.

history.text: About this year Philibert, abbot of Jumieges, driven out of his own house, came to the island of Herio and built a monastery there.
history.source: Vita Filiberti c. 21, in R. Poupardin, Monuments de l'histoire des abbayes de Saint-Philibert (1905)

history.text: This year, on the first day of July, Ansoald, bishop of Poitiers, endowed the house; it was hallowed to the apostles Peter, Andrew and Paul and the martyrs Lawrence and Florent, and given salt works at Ampan on the mainland.
history.source: Poupardin 1905, list of diplomas; I. Cartron, Les peregrinations de saint Philibert (2010) ch. III

history.text: About this year Philibert died and was laid in a marble coffin in the basilica. In his day a ship from Bordeaux brought forty measures of lamp oil, an Irish ship shoes and clothing, and 237 porpoises stranded in a famine year and fed the house.
history.source: Vita Filiberti cc. 27-29 (Poupardin 1905). The year of his death is the common one (?)

history.text: This year pagan ships did much harm among the islands off Aquitaine, and about a hundred and five of the raiders were killed on the shore. The letter names no island.
history.source: Alcuin, letter 184 to Arn (chronicle_793.json 799-aquitaine-islands); that it was Herio is not said (dossier section 8)

history.text: By this year Atto, bishop of Saintes, to whom King Charles had given the monastery, had set the rule to rights there.
history.source: Diploma of Louis and Lothar, 2 August 830, as calendared in Poupardin 1905; Cartron 2010 ch. II. The dates 801 and 804 sometimes given for a rebuilding have no source

history.text: This year the new emperor Louis sent Adalard, abbot of Corbie, his father's cousin and counsellor, to live on the island as an exile. He stayed seven years.
history.source: Cartron 2010 ch. II; Poupardin 1905 (English Wikipedia gives 817-824; Paschasius Radbertus's Life of Adalard was not opened (?))

history.text: This year, on the sixteenth day of March, the emperor gave Abbot Arnulf leave to build a new house at Deas on the mainland as a refuge, because the island house was often laid waste by barbarians.
history.source: Diploma of Louis the Pious, 16 March 819 (Poupardin 1905)

history.text: This year thirteen pirate ships, beaten off from Flanders and the Seine, sacked the island of Bouin across the bay and went home with great plunder.
This year Adalard was called back from the island and given his abbey again.
About this year Abbot Arnulf died and Hilbod was abbot after him.
history.source: Annals of Angouleme and Falco, Chronicon Trenorchiense c. 18, as quoted in Poupardin 1905

history.text: This year, on the eighteenth day of May, King Pippin of Aquitaine confirmed his father's grant: six boats of the abbey go free of toll on the Loire, the Allier, the Cher and the Dordogne.

This year in June the island was left by the general body of the monks for the summer. On the second day of August the emperor took the abbey under his protection, confirmed the fort Abbot Hilbod had built around the monastery, and set its due at six pounds of silver a year.
history.source: Annals of Angouleme 830; diploma of Louis and Lothar, 2 August 830 (Poupardin 1905; Cartron 2010 ch. II)

history.text: This year, on Saint Philibert's own feast, nine ships came to the island. Count Rainald and the abbey's men fought them from the ninth hour until evening; the monks wrote that 484 Northmen fell, and one defender, and many horses.
history.source: Ermentarius, Miracula II.11; Annals of Angouleme (Poupardin 1905). Cartron doubts the date. The Annals of St-Bertin do not mention it, and no plundering is recorded

history.text: This year, on the seventh day of June, the monks dug up Saint Philibert in his marble coffin and took him by ship to Furca, and from there on men's shoulders by Ampan, Varenne and Paulx to Deas, where he came on the eleventh.

About this year Breton ships with yards, sails and anchors came to the abbey's port of Furca to trade: they had brought grain and carried away only salt. One crew took some of the monastery's lead as well, partly by theft and partly by buying on the quiet.
history.source: Ermentarius, Miracula I.81 (Poupardin 1905); the salt works at Scobrit were given to the abbey in 839

history.text: This year, after the sack of Nantes on Saint John's day, the Northmen came to Herio to share the loot and killed each other over it. Captives slipped away when the sea drew back, one with the great Bible of Nantes hung on his neck.
history.source: Chronicon Namnetense c. 7 (ed. Merlet 1896), an eleventh-century telling. The Annals of St-Bertin say only that they wintered on 'a certain island'

history.text: This year in July the monastery of Herio was burned by the Northmen.
history.source: Annals of Angouleme 846, as quoted in Poupardin 1905

history.text: This year, on the thirtieth day of March, Deas was burned. The saint's body went on to Cunault in 858, to Messay in 862, and came to rest at Tournus on the fourteenth day of May 875.
About this year the house on the island was a priory of Tournus. Falco of Tournus wrote that the island had never been wholly without a few monks.
history.source: Falco, Chronicon Trenorchiense c. 22 (Poupardin 1905); fr.wikipedia Abbaye Saint-Philibert de Noirmoutier

eras.text: A quiet island house under an abbot whose name nobody wrote down. The monks keep the hours; the cellarer buys oil for the three lamps and bread corn for the house; Breton and Bordeaux ships lie windbound at Conca and are fed for charity. It is a famine year on the mainland and the island counts its sacks.

The years of the first fear. Heathen ships have been among the islands of Aquitaine and everyone has a cousin who saw them. Bishop Atto of Saintes holds the house and tightens its rule. From 814 a great man lives in the guest house as the emperor's prisoner, and the gate asks strangers more questions.

The summer house is half empty. From early spring to the end of autumn the monks are at Deas; a few brothers stay for the lamps and the salt. From 830 a rampart stands round the monastery with the abbey's own armed men on it, and the lead is off the church roof and lying at Furca for safety. On the feast of 835 there is a fight on the shore and the island wins it.

The saint is gone and the basilica has an empty pit in its floor. A handful of monks, the islanders and their lord remain. Breton ships still come for salt and bring grain. The fort stands with fewer men each year.

After Nantes. The fleet that took the city shares its loot on this shore and fights over it; some summers long ships lie in Conca and their chiefs take a share of the salt as the abbot once did (?). In July 846 the monastery burns.

Whoever holds the island holds the salt. The islanders rake the beds for their own lord in a quiet year and for a ship's chief in a bad one, and sell to anyone who lands with grain. Two or three monks keep a roofed corner of the church (Falco). Fleets go up and down the Loire; Nantes is a Northmen's town from 919. No king's man comes here.

The Loire is the Bretons' and the Franks' again after Alan Barbetorte takes Nantes back. The island belongs to its lords on the mainland shore. The church is patched; the old fort is a grassy bank with sheep on it. Salt goes north in Breton hulls every autumn.

A priory of Tournus: a prior and a few monks sent from the house on the Saone where the saint now lies, come to keep his empty grave. The lords of La Garnache hold the island and talk of a tower. More salt beds are cut each year, and English and Norman ships are seen in the bay (?).

sites.name: Conca, the shell bay
sites.see: A half-moon of pale sand on the island's north side, low grey rocks at either horn, the open bay beyond and the Loire shore a blue line far off. Two or three ships ride to stone anchors waiting for a wind; boats lie on the sand with their yards lowered. Behind the beach a path climbs through tamarisk to the monastery's west gate. Wind in the rigging, oystercatchers, the smell of weed drying on the tide line.
sites.source: Ermentarius, Miracula I.81 and II.9: 'our island's port called Conca', where ships anchor and wait for a wind; II.11: the west gate leads to it. La Conche, on the north side (Poupardin 1905)

sites.name: The salt heaps
sites.see: Above the tide line at Conca, on trodden sand: grey salt in heaps the height of a man's knee, each under a mat of rushes weighted with stones, and a row of rush baskets for carrying it. A wooden measure stands on a plank; beside it whatever the last ship brought, grain in sacks, a few jars. Women with rakes, a monk with a tally stick, gulls walking between the heaps.
sites.source: No market is recorded on the island (dossier section 8): selling on the beach is the game's (?). The trade itself is Ermentarius, Miracula I.81: grain in, 'only salt' out. Pennies and halfpennies pass at the abbey's market at Deas (I.71)

sites.name: The west gate
sites.see: A gate of heavy timber in a wall of dry stone, facing the sea path, with a bench outside for those who wait and a cross on a post a spear's cast before it. A brother sits in the gate with a loaf basket. From 830 an earth rampart with a palisade runs off on either hand and a man with a spear looks down from above the gate.
sites.source: Ermentarius, Miracula II.11: monastery and fort share a west gate, towards Conca. The porter is the Rule of St Benedict c. 66. The cross marking how near women may come is recorded for Deas (I.71); here it is supposed (?)

sites.name: Saint Philibert's basilica
sites.see: A long low church of small squared stone with a roof of grey lead that shines after rain. Inside it is dark and cool: at the east end a white marble coffin on a step, three lamps burning at its head by day and by night, a staff laid along it, and a wooden frame with carrying poles leaning against the wall. Sick people sit on the floor with a hand on the stone. After June 836 the step is bare and there is a pit beside it; after 846 the roof is open to the sky.
sites.source: Ermentarius, Miracula I.2 (the marble coffin, the carrying frame, wine in which the staff was washed) and II.8 (three lamps always lit; 'the other church' near by). The look of the building is not known (?); the lead is I.81

sites.name: The cellarer's store
sites.see: A stone room half sunk in the ground beside the kitchen, with one door and a slit of light. Oil jars stand shoulder to shoulder in sand along one wall; sacks of corn hang from the beams out of reach of rats; lumps of lead are stacked like loaves in the corner. A monk with a wax tablet stands in the doorway and looks at what you carry before he looks at you.
sites.source: Vita Filiberti cc. 26-27: the kitchen, the cellarer's store, the lamp oil from Bordeaux, the fat of a stranded sea beast for the lamps. The lead in lumps is Ermentarius, Miracula I.81

sites.name: The guest house
sites.see: A thatched house outside the cloister wall with a hearth in the middle and straw-filled bed frames along both sides. A basin and a towel wait by the door. Windbound seamen sleep at one end; at the other a table under a small window holds an ink horn, a knife and a few leaves weighted with a stone. From 814 to 821 a tall old monk writes there every morning and a king's man sits by the door.
sites.source: Vita Filiberti cc. 27, 29: guests at the abbot's table; windbound Breton ships given two beasts, flour and bread. The Rule of St Benedict c. 53. Adalard's exile: Cartron 2010 ch. II

sites.name: The abbot's table
sites.see: A plain room off the cloister with one long table, a bench on each side and a chair at the end with arms. A book lies open on a stand for the reading at meals. Fish, beans, bread and a jug of thin wine; nobody speaks while the reader reads. Through the door the cloister garth is green and a brother is drawing water.
sites.source: Vita Filiberti cc. 26-27 (the abbot's table, guests, a cloister). The abbot of 793 is not known; from 819 the abbot is on the island only before Easter and after the autumn (diploma of 830)

sites.name: The clay beds
sites.see: On the lagoon side, where the sand bar joins the two islets: shallow square beds cut in grey clay, each a hand deep in still water with a white skin forming at the edges, low banks between them and a sluice of planks to the tide. Rakes with long handles, small cones of wet salt draining on the banks, a hut of turf. Flat light, flies, the sour smell of mud in the sun.
sites.source: Salt beds on the island itself are supposed, not attested (Cartron 2010 ch. III; dossier section 8) (?). The abbey's attested works are on the mainland: Ampan from 677, Scobrit from 839. goods_793.json sea_salt; works_793.json salt_pan

sites.name: Abbot Hilbod's fort
sites.see: An earth bank faced with stone and topped with stakes, drawn in a ring round the monastery, with a ditch outside that fills at spring tides. Men of the abbey's household walk the top with spears and round shields; horses are tied inside the gate. By 950 it is a grassed bank with a gap where the gate stood, and children run along it.
sites.source: Diploma of 2 August 830: a castrum built by Hilbod around the monastery, guarded by the abbey's own men; Falco c. 18: a strong citadel with a rampart. Its plan is not known (?). Horsemen in 835: Ermentarius II.11

sites.name: The old graves
sites.see: On the north shore, a short walk east of Conca: broken walls of thin red brick standing knee high in the grass, and among them stone coffins, some with their lids askew and sand drifted in. A small chapel of Saint Hilary stands over the newest graves. Sea pinks, a view straight out to the open water, and no sound but the wind.
sites.source: Le Vieil: a large Gallo-Roman site reused as a Merovingian burial ground, with a chapel of St Hilary over the graves, undated (Cartron 2010 ch. III); stone coffins from it are shown in the castle keep (fr.wikipedia Ile de Noirmoutier)

sites.name: The wood on the east head
sites.see: A head of rock some three men's height above the bay, covered with wind-bent oaks and holly, the only trees on the island. Below it a cleft in the rock where the founder is said to have prayed. From the top the whole bay lies open: Bouin low on the water to the east, the Loire shore north of it, and any sail a half day before it arrives.
sites.source: The wooded head of La Chaize, about 15 m high (fr.wikipedia Ile de Noirmoutier); Saint Philibert's cave there is tradition only (the parish's page). Holm oaks are today's wood; what grew there in 793 is not known (?)

sites.name: The western flats
sites.see: At low water the sea goes out of sight to the west and leaves a plain of ribbed sand, black reefs and pools. Islanders walk it with baskets and forks for cockles and set stake nets in the gullies. The shore is white with gulls and waders, so many that when they rise the light changes. Far out a small steep islet stands off the north-west point.
sites.source: Flats and reefs west and south that dry at low water; the islet of Le Pilier (fr.wikipedia Ile de Noirmoutier). The birds: Ermentarius, Miracula II.10. Stranded porpoises and a sea beast: Vita Filiberti cc. 27-28

people.name: Vitalis
people.trait: The house's cellarer: counts in jars and sacks, forgets no ship that ever fed the island, and is mean with everything but bread for strangers.
people.want: Oil enough that the three lamps never go out in his time, and corn in the beams before the autumn gales.
people.fear: A dark lamp at the saint's head on his watch; after 799, a sail he does not know.
people.voice: Dry and exact, in the Romance of the bay with church Latin for numbers. Asks what you have aboard before he asks your name.
people.looks: About forty-five, thin, a tonsure gone grey, a patched black habit kilted up for work, a wax tablet on a cord at his belt and oil stains to the elbow.
knows: what the house will pay for oil, corn, wine, lead and shoes, and what it will give in salt
which ships have called since Easter and what they carried
the old stories of the house: the Bordeaux oil ship, the Irish ship, the porpoises
who is abbot's man on the mainland at Furca

ties.note: Took him as a boy and taught him to count sacks; thinks his riddles a waste of wax.
Pays the pilot in bread and trusts his word on a ship's draught.
The rakers are paid in corn, and in a hungry year the corn is late.
The house has bought its lamp oil from Bordeaux since the founder's day and is a season behind in paying (?).
Sells him salt for Saint-Germain's fish and takes his riddle leaves for the salt brother.
Has never met him: sends salt up the Loire to Saint Martin's at Tours from 796 and gets letters of thanks.
sends the old bishop of Nantes salt at Michaelmas, with a list of what the island lacks (?)
says her shed sells last year's sweepings as bay salt, and buys her ale for the abbey's carters all the same (?)

lines.greet: God keep you. What is under your deck boards? If it is corn or oil, come in. If it is anything else, come in anyway.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the small boat. You draw less water than my pilot said and you carry more than I believed.
lines.greet_friend: Sit. Your sacks are still in my tally from last year and I have told the brothers whose corn they are eating.
rumour: The harvest failed on the mainland again. Men come down to the shore opposite and shout across for bread.
A Bordeaux ship should have been here by Saint John's with oil. Either the wind is foul in the south or the price has gone up.
They say heathen ships fell on an English island before midsummer and killed monks at the altar. We are an island of monks. I notice these things.
lines.saying: The founder fed a whole year on porpoises. I would rather not ask him for it twice.
lines.farewell: Go with the ebb, not against it. And if you pass Bordeaux, tell them the lamps are hungry.

people.source: invented; the office is in the Life (Vita Filiberti c. 27: the cellarer and his store) and in the Rule of St Benedict c. 31

people.name: Natalis
people.trait: The brother who keeps the salt: sunburnt, cheerful, schooled for a while at Tours, and unable to hand over a sack without setting a riddle first.
people.want: Somebody on this island who can answer him back; failing that, a merchant who comes again.
people.fear: That the house will leave the island and the salt for good, and that he will be the one told to stay.
people.voice: Quick and teasing, hands always moving. Puts a question where another man would put a price.
people.looks: Late twenties in 793, brown as a nut, a black habit white to the knee with salt, bare feet, a long wooden rake over his shoulder and a folded leaf tucked in his sleeve.
knows: the price of salt here by the month, and when the beds will be ready
Aldhelm's riddle of the wine cask, on a leaf sent from Quentovic by the monk Meginbert, and where the next one is kept
which summers the monks will be away, from 819
the ebbs on the lagoon side

ties.note: The cellarer's man; every sack he sells is cut on Vitalis's tally.
She rakes better than he does and tells him so.
Sat two winters in the school at Saint Martin's after 796 and learned riddling there. Alcuin taught him; the tie runs from the master.
The first seaman he has met who can read a leaf; he saves the hard ones for him.
The Frisian wine shipper at Mainz who keeps the next leaf; they have never met, and send word by salt ships (?).
Saint-Germain's monk at the wic buys the island's salt and sent the cask leaf here by way of the cellarer.
From 825 his abbot, who leaves him on the island every summer because the salt cannot be left.
ferried over the Loire on the way to Tours and back; pays half the fare in riddles, which the ferryman has begun to answer (?)
from 814 brings the exile riddles and the bay's gossip, and has his Latin corrected for it
tells the young scribe which of the saint's wonders the islanders tell differently

lines.greet: A new hull. Good. Before we talk of sacks: I am made by sun and sea and I die in water. No? You are standing in it.
lines.greet_again: You came back. Then you can have the one about the cask. I have been keeping it dry for you.
lines.greet_friend: My Frisian. The beds are ready, the best heap is yours, and I have a question you will hate.
rumour: The brothers at Tours write a new hand, round and clear. A child could read it. I can nearly write it.
The house goes to the mainland at the first spring tide after Easter and leaves four of us with the lamps. I am always one of the four.
The lead is off the church roof and across the water at Furca. When it rains the saint gets wet and the abbot says that is better than a heathen with a ladle.
lines.saying: Salt keeps meat a winter and a riddle keeps a guest an evening. I deal in both.
lines.farewell: Think on it at sea. A man answers better when he has nothing else to look at.

people.source: invented; riddles_793.json gives the wine-cask riddle (riddle_aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria) to 'a monk of the salt pans' at Herio, 793-835. Alcuin was abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours 796-804

people.name: Ursus
people.trait: An islander and a steersman: knows the ebbs of the bay as other men know their fields, takes his time, and has never yet touched bottom with another man's ship.
people.want: A boy of his own blood to learn the marks; his sister's grandson will do when he is old enough to hold a pole.
people.fear: Calm weather in summer. A flat sea is a road for anyone.
people.voice: Slow, with long silences while he looks at the water. Names days by the moon and distances by tides.
people.looks: Past forty in 793, broad and short, a face like a boot, a hooded cloak of undyed wool stiff with salt, bare legs, a sounding pole marked with rings of red wool.
knows: when the monastery's channel dries and when a small boat can lie against the gate path
the fast run to Furca before a north-west wind, and the strait at the south end that closes the bay
which Breton steersmen are in the bay and who their bow lookouts are
where a ship went on the reef and why

ties.note: His sister.
Her grandson; he teaches the child the marks from the time he can walk the flats.
The cellarer pays him in bread and asks him what each ship draws.
The Loire pilots say the bay men cannot read a river; the bay men say the same of them at sea (?).
Has heard of the pilot of the Maas mouth from Frisians in for salt and sends him his greeting by any ship going north.
hands the salt boats on to him at the Garonne mouth, and has his news back by the same hulls (?)

lines.greet: You came in on the last of the flood. That was luck or sense. Next time ask me and it will be sense.
lines.greet_again: The small Frisian boat. She sits well. Who taught your steersman to lay her head to the swell like that?
lines.greet_friend: I saw your sail from the east head at noon and told my sister to put fish on. Come ashore.
rumour: Three Breton ships are windbound in the bay with corn. Their steersmen are drinking the abbot's charity and praying for north-west.
The bar has moved a boat's length since the winter. I have not told the Bretons yet.
A ship like a wall came up from the island to the south once and turned away. The birds rose off the flats and they took them for men.
lines.saying: Our men cannot always reach the island for the ebbs. A stranger with a calm sea can, any day he likes.
lines.farewell: Third night of the moon you will have water over the bar at dawn. Not before.

people.source: invented; steersmen (gubernator) and bow lookouts (proreta) are in Ermentarius, Miracula I.81; the ebbs and the calm sea are the king's council of 836 (I.1); the ship 'like a wall' and the birds are II.10

people.name: Maura
people.trait: A fisherman's widow who leads the rakers on the salt beds: an islander under the island's own lord, not the monks' woman, and she will remind a monk of it.
people.want: Her corn paid on the day it is owed, and her grandson given a trade that does not drown him.
people.fear: A hungry winter with the house's store shut; the day the monks stop coming back.
people.voice: Loud, quick, laughs at her own bargains. Calls every merchant 'my son' until he cheats her.
people.looks: Mid thirties in 793, strong arms, a brown wool dress kilted to the knee, a linen cloth tied over her hair, salt sores on her shins and a rake she lets nobody else carry.
knows: which heap is this week's salt and which is last year's swept up
what the islanders want that the monks do not buy: needles, knives, cloth, a pot
how near the gate a woman may come, to the step
who on the island has a boat to sell or a son who wants to go to sea

ties.note: Her brother, the pilot.
Her grandson, born about 812; she raises him on the beds.
The only monk she will take orders from, because he rakes beside her.
He counts her corn by the level measure and she wants it heaped.
a widow in the wine city who sends a jar by the salt boats; Maura sends back her best grey salt and has never seen her (?)

lines.greet: A stranger with a clean boat. My son, that grey heap is this week's. The white one the monk shows you was swept off the floor.
lines.greet_again: You again. Did the salt keep your meat? Then you owe me a good word in the north.
lines.greet_friend: Here is my Frisian. Boy, fetch the good measure, not the one we keep for Bretons.
rumour: The cellarer pays in corn and the corn is late. If you have a sack to spare, sell it to us on the sand, not at the gate.
I may walk as far as the cross before the gate and no nearer. The saint is not afraid of women. The brothers are.
My man went out for a stranded fish the length of this beach and the tide took him. The monks got the fat for their lamps.
lines.saying: The sea gives salt to those who wait and takes those who hurry.
lines.farewell: Come after the Assumption next year. It is cheapest then and I am in the best temper.

people.source: invented; the islanders (insulani) with a lord of their own are Ermentarius, Miracula I.1; no islander's name survives. The stranded sea beast and its lamp fat: Vita Filiberti c. 27. Women kept from the monastery: I.29, I.71, of Deas; here supposed (?)

people.name: Adalard
people.trait: Abbot of Corbie, the old emperor's cousin and counsellor, sent here by the new emperor to be out of the way: courteous, tireless, and not in the least resigned.
people.want: Letters carried to Corbie and answers brought back; news of his brother Wala and his sister; to see his own house again.
people.fear: To die on a sand bar with the work unfinished, and that the young men he trained will be scattered.
people.voice: Clear court Frankish, or Latin, or the Romance of the place, whichever you have. Asks exact questions and waits for the whole answer.
people.looks: Past sixty, tall and spare, white hair round a tonsure, a plain black habit worn like a lord's cloak, ink on his fingers, a small book always in his left hand.
knows: the court as it was under the old emperor, and who rules it now
the road and the river way to Corbie on the Somme, and who keeps the gate there
how an abbey's stores should be ordered: he has written it all down for his own
who on this island reports to the count

ties.note: A boy in the school at Corbie when Adalard was sent away; after 821 Adalard sends him to the new house in Saxony (?).
Alcuin wrote to him as a friend and gave him a pet name at court (?); Alcuin is ten years dead when he comes here.
The salt monk brings him riddles and gossip; Adalard corrects his Latin.
The count of the Breton march answers to the emperor for what comes and goes on this coast, an exile's letters with it (?).
Corbie's man in the Channel port forwards what reaches him; he is Adalard's own monk still (?).

lines.greet: You are from the Rhine mouth. Then you know Dorestat, and tolls, and how long a letter takes to the Somme. Sit down and tell me all three.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Good. I have counted the days since you sailed, and I had them right to within two.
lines.greet_friend: My friend. The man by the door has gone to eat. We have as long as a bowl of beans takes him.
rumour: The emperor is a pious man and has pious men about him. I was one of the old kind. We were less pious and got more done.
This house has its lamps, its salt and its fear, in that order. In ten years the order will be turned about.
My brother Wala was a count and is made a monk. He is learning that a cowl is not a quiet thing to wear.
lines.saying: An exile has one comfort: nobody asks him for anything, so he can at last finish what he is writing.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you come to Corbie before I do, tell the porter that the abbot asks whether the bees were moved.

people.source: Adalard of Corbie (about 751 to 2 January 827), Charlemagne's cousin; exiled to the island 814-821 (Cartron 2010 ch. II; Poupardin 1905; English Wikipedia gives 817-824). His Life by Paschasius Radbertus was not opened (?); the watcher at the door and his words are the game's

people.name: Hilbod
people.trait: The abbot who built a rampart round his monastery and then carried his saint away from it: practical, unsentimental, a man who measures a thing before he mourns it.
people.want: The founder's bones where no heathen can dig them up and throw them in the sea; a ship and bearers he can trust for the day it must be done.
people.fear: Being the abbot under whom the saint was scattered; and, after it, being the abbot who left.
people.voice: Short sentences, no ornament. Thanks God briefly and men by name.
people.looks: About fifty, square and weathered, more like a steward than a monk, a black habit with the hem muddy, a ring, and a rod he measures things with out of habit.
knows: what the emperor's and King Pippin's charters give the house: the fort, six toll-free boats, the six pounds a year
the road from Furca by Ampan, Varenne and Paulx to Deas
how many armed men the abbey keeps and what they cost
what Count Rainald will and will not do for the island

ties.note: The young monk writes down what the abbot does and why; the abbot reads it and strikes out the adjectives.
Leaves him with the salt every summer and brings him a new leaf from Deas every autumn.
The count of Herbauge fought for the island on the saint's feast in 835.
The islanders stay when the monks go; the abbot knows what that will cost them.
Abbot Hilduin of Saint-Denis, the emperor's archchaplain, is the patron to whom the house sends its book of miracles.
the bishop of Nantes spoke for him when people called the saint's going a faint heart
the Bordeaux merchant takes the house's salt on a year's credit and has paid every Martinmas (?)

lines.greet: You are the Frisian the salt brother talks about. He says you answer him. Nobody else does. What does your ship carry, at the most?
lines.greet_again: Good. I wanted a man who has seen this beach at low water and come back anyway.
lines.greet_friend: Come in. I am in the cloister four weeks a year now and I do not waste them on strangers.
rumour: The king's council said it plainly: our men cannot always reach the island, and the heathen can whenever the sea is calm.
I built the wall. It held on the feast day. A wall that holds once teaches the other side to bring more ships.
King Pippin's assembly has agreed. I will not say to what until the tide table is settled.
lines.saying: A saint can be carried. An island cannot. So one decides which of the two the house is.
lines.farewell: Go with God. Be in Conca on the tenth day after Pentecost, at the top of the flood, if you want to be remembered here.

people.source: Hilbod, abbot from 824/825, still abbot in February 856 (Annals of Angouleme; Poupardin 1905); built the castrum (diploma of 2 August 830) and moved the saint, 7-11 June 836 (Ermentarius, Miracula I.1-2). In 836 Easter fell on 9 April and Pentecost on 28 May, so the seventh of June is the tenth day after it. His birth, death and looks are not recorded

people.name: Ermentarius
people.trait: A young monk with a good hand and a memory for small true things: the price of a measure of wine, what a liar swore by, how many birds stood on the shore.
people.want: To write down every wonder of the saint before the people who saw it die; a witness who was there, and will say so.
people.fear: That the house will go on moving until nobody remembers the island at all.
people.voice: Earnest, careful, fond of 'unless I am mistaken'. Wants names, days and hours and writes them on his tablet as you speak.
people.looks: Not yet thirty, slight, short-sighted, a clean black habit, a wax tablet in a leather case round his neck and a stylus behind his ear.
knows: every cure at the tomb and who was cured
the fight on the feast day in 835 as the defenders told it, and the dream a monk at Corbie had the night before
the story of the Breton lead thieves and the horseman with three spears
what a sextarius of wine costs at the market before the gate at Deas

ties.note: His abbot; later he is abbot himself, far from the sea.
The salt brother tells him which stories the islanders tell differently.
He sends the first book of the Miracles to Abbot Hilduin of Saint-Denis about 838-840.
The islander who can tell him what happens on the island after the monks have gone.
asked the bishop what he saw of the saint's road, and wrote the answer down nearly as given

lines.greet: You were at sea on the feast day? Then tell me what you saw, slowly, and the hour. I am writing it all down.
lines.greet_again: I have you in my tablet already. A Frisian, a small boat, salt. Is there anything since that I should add?
lines.greet_friend: Good, a witness I trust. Sit. I will read you what I wrote and you will tell me where I have made it too fine.
rumour: A man at Deas swore by the saint that a halfpenny was his own, drank his wine and brought it all up at the door. I saw the wine.
Bretons took our lead from Furca, part stolen and part bought on the quiet. They had no wind until they brought it back. It came back in sheets.
The night before the fight a brother at Corbie dreamed our saint in white with a golden sword, going out by the west gate.
lines.saying: A measure of wine was a penny that year, unless I am mistaken.
lines.farewell: God speed you. If you hear anything of the saint on your road, bring it to me. I pay in prayers, and the abbot in salt.

people.source: Ermentarius, monk of the house, eyewitness of 836 and author of De translationibus et miraculis sancti Filiberti (book I about 838-840, book II after 862); later abbot (Poupardin 1905). The lines draw on Miracula I.71, I.81, II.11. That he was on the island from 830 is supposed (?)

people.name: Martinus
people.trait: The islander who stayed: Maura's grandson, raised on the salt beds and taught the ebbs by old Ursus. He sells to whoever lands and keeps his opinions for those he has known a long time.
people.want: The beds worked, his people fed, and a buyer who comes every year, whoever came in the last ship.
people.fear: A fleet that does not want salt. A chief who wants salters instead.
people.voice: Quiet, level, watches your hands. Speaks a little Breton and, after 843, a few hard words of Norse for numbers.
people.looks: Mid twenties in 836, lean and sun-dark, a short hooded tunic, bare feet, his grandmother's rake, and on a thong round his neck a little bag with a thread of the cloth that lay on the saint's coffin.
knows: who holds the island this year and what share of the salt he takes
when long ships are in the bay and where they lie
the ebbs, as Ursus taught them, and where a small boat can lie unseen on the lagoon side
what became of the captives of Nantes, and what one of them carried

ties.note: His grandmother, who raised him on the beds.
The old pilot taught him the marks; the tie runs from the old man.
Sends word to the monks at Deas of what happens on the island.
Still calls himself the saint's man, and keeps a lamp lit in the empty church when there is fat for it.
Bishop Gunhard of Nantes, killed in his church on Saint John's day 843; Martinus hid one of his clerks.
sells to him after the monks are gone, and is asked no questions about who else buys

lines.greet: You are the house my grandmother sold to. She said a small boat and a straight measure. Show me the measure.
lines.greet_again: The same hull. Good. Lie on the lagoon side this time. Fewer eyes.
lines.greet_friend: I kept the best heap covered since the Assumption and told three Bretons it was spoken for. It was.
rumour: The monks went with the saint in my twenty-fourth summer. Two came back to mind the lamps. The salt did not notice.
After Nantes they shared the plunder on this sand and fought over it. We buried eleven of theirs. Nobody asked us to.
Whoever sits in the abbot's chair takes one sack in ten. The abbot took it for God. This one takes it for his ship. The salt weighs the same.
lines.saying: Salt has no lord. It only has whoever is standing on the bank.
lines.farewell: Go out by the south gully on the ebb. If you see more than three sails together, you never knew me.

people.source: invented; islanders still live on the island about 838-840 (Ermentarius, Miracula I.81) and it was never wholly without a few monks (Falco c. 22). The loot of Nantes shared and fought over on Herio: Chronicon Namnetense c. 7. That a ship's chief took a share of the salt is the game's reading of the spine (?). The thread of cloth at his neck: the sick touched the coffin, its carrying frame or its cloth (Miracula I.2)

stories.title: Oil for three lamps
stories.summary: In the hungry summer of 793 the island has salt and nothing else: the corn in the cellarer's beams is nearly gone and the Bordeaux oil ship has not come. Vitalis will pay for corn and oil in salt at a rate no mainland market gives, and he remembers who fed the house and who made it beg.
stories.picture: A thin monk with a wax tablet standing in a sunken stone doorway, behind him a row of oil jars in sand, most of them tipped to show they are empty; in the dark beyond, three small flames.

beats.text: Vitalis shows you the store without being asked: nine jars empty, two full, the corn sacks hanging slack. He names his price in salt for a boatload of rye or wheat, and a better one for oil, and says the lamps have never gone out since the founder died.
Maura and the rakers want the corn too, on the sand, and will give more salt for it than the cellarer because they are hungrier. Whichever you sell to, the other hears of it before the tide turns.

At Bordeaux the oil comes up from the south by river and cart and is dear this year. The seller knows the island house: forty measures went there in the founder's day and the debt for last year's jars is still open. He will ship on your hull if you stand surety, or sell to you outright.
At the Loire city corn is under the king's price and watched. A boat loading for the saint's island is let go; a boat loading for anywhere else is asked questions.
You come back with what you have. If it is oil, Vitalis fills the third lamp himself, with the church-keeper holding the wick, and says nothing at all until it is burning.
Saint Germain's man on the Canche buys the island's salt for the abbey's fish. He has heard whether there are two lamps or three, and from whose boat the corn came.

endings.how: You brought corn at the king's price and oil from Bordeaux, and took salt for both.
endings.text: The lamps burn. Vitalis cuts your house's mark on the doorpost of the store, low down where the abbot will not see it, and from that year the island's best salt is held back for your sail.
endings.reward: Sets hy_fed_poor; the unlocks herio.cellarers_tally and herio.guests_bench; a full hold of salt at about half the autumn price; Vitalis and Natalis as fast friends.

endings.how: You sold the corn to the islanders on the sand for the higher price in salt.
endings.text: Nobody starves and the rakers bless you. The cellarer buys his corn from the next Breton, late and dear, and for a year counts your sacks twice. Maura's people remember it for three generations.
endings.reward: A third more salt than the cellarer would have given; Maura and, later, Martinus as fast friends (the unlock herio.lagoon_berth); Vitalis cool until you bring oil.

endings.how: You held the corn for the highest offer and took the house's lead in part payment.
endings.text: It is a great price. One lamp is put out to spare the oil, for the first time since the founder, and every brother knows whose bargain did it. The story is told at Tours before you are home.
endings.reward: Lead and salt worth about twice the corn; sets hy_sold_dear; the monks of the Loire are wary of you, and act:lodge and act:provision are closed to you here until alms are given at the tomb.

stories.reward: The island's tally and its best salt for a lifetime, or one very good cargo and a cold gate.

stories.title: The leaf in the salt
stories.summary: The riddle of salt, had at Quentovic or Dorestad, points to where salt is made. On the clay beds the salt brother Natalis keeps the next leaf, Aldhelm's riddle of the wine cask, and gives it only to someone who has answered the first. Its answer sends the merchant up the Rhine to Mogontia, then to Colonia, and at last to the October fair of Saint-Denis.
stories.picture: A sunburnt monk sitting on the bank of a salt bed with a rake across his knees, holding out a folded leaf between two fingers, a boy sailor reading over the merchant's shoulder, cones of salt white behind them.

beats.text: A monk on his abbey's business sets the riddle of the thing born of sun and sea that dies in water. The answer is salt, and he says the brother who has the next leaf rakes it with his own hands, on an island south of the Loire.

Natalis asks the salt riddle before he will sell a sack. Answered, he laughs, wipes his hands and brings out the leaf: a thing split with wedges by a countryman, that holds what makes men foolish. It is in Latin. Beornwine can read it slowly; so can any monk, for a favour.
If the exile Adalard is in the guest house he will read the leaf aloud and correct its Latin, and will not give the answer: he says a merchant who cannot name a cask has no business loading one.
After the monks leave the island the leaf is kept by a salt merchant of the Loire city, who had it from Natalis with a sack of the last good salt.
Where the casks come from: the third leaf, the glass cup, waits among the wine sellers on the Rhine, and the fourth, pepper, at Colonia.
At the fair of Saint-Denis the whole chain, answered, is worth the right to sell pepper there.

endings.how: You answered the cask riddle yourself, there or on a later call.
endings.text: Natalis claps salt off his hands and says you have cost him an evening's sport. He gives you the name of the man at Mogontia and a sack over the measure, and asks for the next leaf to be read to him if you ever come back.
endings.reward: The riddle riddle_aldhelm_78_cupa_vinaria solved and the next link of salt_to_pepper open; a small purse (rw_silver_small); Natalis as a fast friend, with a new riddle on every call.

endings.how: You could not read it, and paid a monk to read it and tell you the answer.
endings.text: You have the answer and Natalis knows how you got it. He sells you salt at the common price and keeps his hard ones for other men. The chain still runs on to Mogontia.
endings.reward: The next link open; no purse; Natalis easy but not a friend.

endings.how: You took salt and never answered.
endings.text: The leaf stays in his sleeve. Each time you call he asks again, a little more gently. After 835 it goes to Namnetis with the last sacks, and the asking starts over with a stranger.
endings.reward: Nothing lost: the riddle waits, here until 835 and at Namnetis after.

stories.reward: The second link of the salt-to-pepper chain, and a monk who saves his best questions for you.

stories.title: The emperor's cousin
stories.summary: From 814 to 821 Adalard of Corbie lives in the guest house as the emperor's exile. He wants letters carried to his abbey on the Somme and one small book brought back from its chest, and a king's man sits by the door to see that neither happens. What the merchant does is remembered at Corbie, at court, and in the north where Corbie's pupils go.
stories.picture: A tall white-haired monk writing at a small window, a folded letter held low under the table towards the viewer; in the doorway behind him a bored armed man eating beans from a bowl.

beats.text: Adalard asks about Dorestad, tolls and how long a letter takes to the Somme. On the second evening, while the watcher eats, he asks whether your boat calls at Quentovic, and whether you can keep a thing dry.

The king's man at the gate has his own offer: the count pays for knowing who carries the old abbot's letters and to whom. He does not threaten. He says it is only a matter of which lord a merchant wants to be known to.

Corbie's agent in the port takes the letter without surprise and is back in eight days with a book the length of a hand, sewn in oiled linen: the abbot's own notes on the ordering of a house, which he wants beside him to finish.
The count's clerk at the Loire city asks, in passing, what a Frisian was doing in the guest house of an island of monks for three nights.
You come back. He weighs the book in his hand before he opens it, and reads the first page standing.
The exile is abbot again. A monk of Corbie finds your ship in the harbour with a message that begins with the day you sailed from Conca, right to within two.
Abbot Hilduin, fresh from court, is asked about the old emperor's cousin on his sand bar. He says the emperor is merciful, and turns the talk to parchment.

endings.how: You carried the letter north and the book south, and said nothing to the count's men.
endings.text: He finishes his writing on the island. When he is called back in 821 he does not forget a hull: Corbie's cellarer buys from your house first, and a young monk of that school, going north to the Danes, asks for you by name.
endings.reward: Sets bk_carried and bk_knows_worth; the unlock herio.adalards_word; Adalard a fast friend until his death in 827; Anskar friendly at first meeting.

endings.how: You took the letter and showed it to the count's clerk.
endings.text: The clerk reads it, finds nothing but questions about bees and granaries, and pays you all the same. The watcher at the door is changed for a sharper one. Adalard greets you as before and never again asks you anything.
endings.reward: 120 pennies and the count's goodwill on the Loire (standing with the king's men); Adalard and the monks of Corbie closed to this merchant; Natalis keeps his riddles to himself for a year.

endings.how: You told him plainly that you would not carry it.
endings.text: He nods, says a merchant must know his own hold, and goes on asking about tolls. He finds another ship before the summer is out.
endings.reward: Nothing gained or lost; his talk of the court stays open to you.

stories.reward: A friend at Corbie and in its school for the north, or the count's silver and a closed door.

stories.title: The saint goes ashore
stories.summary: On the saint's feast in 835 nine ships come and the island beats them. Abbot Hilbod draws the other lesson: next year, on the seventh day of June, the founder leaves in his marble coffin by ship for Furca and the mainland. He needs a hull that knows the ebbs, and the islanders who are staying need someone to tell them what they are being left with.
stories.picture: A white stone coffin on a wooden frame being walked down a beach on the shoulders of eight monks towards a small boat held in the shallows, an abbot with a measuring rod ahead of it, islanders standing silent along the tide line with their rakes.

beats.text: After the feast: trampled sand, dead horses, the abbey's men counting. One defender is dead. The monks say four hundred and eighty-four of the heathen; the men who dug the pit say fewer and do not argue. Count Rainald rides off the island at the next ebb.

Hilbod asks what your ship carries at the most, and what a marble coffin with a man in it weighs. He has King Pippin's leave. He wants it done in one tide, between the ebb that bares the channel and the flood that floats you off.
Martinus and the rakers ask you what the monks will not tell them: is the saint going, and is the wall to be manned after. They are not coming to Deas. Nobody has asked them.

The seventh day of June. The coffin comes down the path from the west gate on its frame, the brothers singing. It goes aboard a ship at the top of the flood and runs to Furca before a north-west wind.
At the Loire city they say the saint walked to Deas on men's shoulders in four days and that the sick were healed along the road. The bishop asks whether anybody is left on the island to say Mass.
A pit in the floor, a bare step, one lamp where there were three. Martinus trims it. He asks what the monks said about him at Furca.
A wine and salt dealer at Bordeaux has always paid the island's abbot at Martinmas. He asks who is to be paid now: the monks at Deas, or the people raking the salt.
A book has come to Abbot Hilduin from the monks who left the island: the saint's journey and his wonders, by a young scribe. The abbot reads it with a pen in his hand.

endings.how: You gave your ship for the crossing to Furca and brought her in on the tide Hilbod named.
endings.text: Ermentarius writes that the sea lay flat for the saint. He does not name the ship, but the house knows it: wherever the body rests afterwards, at Deas, Cunault or Tournus, a merchant of your line is a guest of Saint Philibert.
endings.reward: Sets herio_saint_carried; the unlock herio.saints_guest; a great deed among churchmen of the Loire; 240 pennies' worth of salt from the abbot's own store.

endings.how: You let another hull take the saint and carried the abbey's goods and lead to Furca for a fee.
endings.text: It is honest work and well paid. The lead lies at Furca, where Bretons will find it in three years. The monks thank you as they would a carter.
endings.reward: 180 pennies and first refusal on the abbey's lead; Hilbod easy; no place in the book.

endings.how: You told the islanders the truth before the day and helped them move the last of the store to the lagoon side.
endings.text: The monks sail without your help and without their third heap of salt, which is under rushes in the dunes. Hilbod knows who told. Martinus knows too, and that is worth more on this island for the next forty years.
endings.reward: The unlock herio.lagoon_berth; Martinus a fast friend, and his word passed to his children; Hilbod cool; salt at the islanders' own price.

stories.reward: A name among the saint's people on the mainland, or among the people he left behind.

stories.title: Whoever holds the island
stories.summary: On Saint John's day 843 the Northmen storm Nantes and kill the bishop in his church; afterwards they come to Herio to share the loot and fight over it. Among their captives is a clerk of the cathedral with its great Bible tied on his neck. The salt is still there, the islanders still rake it, and somebody else now takes the tenth sack.
stories.picture: Low water at dusk: long ships drawn up on a beach with fires beside them and men quarrelling over a heap of church plate, and in the foreground, out on the wet flats, a small figure wading away with a great square book bound to his back.

beats.text: The city after the feast: the cathedral door hanging, blood on the floor, the people who were not killed carried downriver in the ships. The canons ask every hull bound seaward whether it is going by the salt island.

Martinus meets you below the tide line and says: lie on the lagoon side. The fleet is in Conca, the plunder is on the sand and they have been killing each other over it since yesterday. They want bread and wine and will pay in things that came off altars.

In the salt hut, under the rakes, a clerk of Nantes with a book as big as a door tied to him by its own straps. He went when the sea drew back and the guards were drunk or fighting. Martinus cannot keep him past the next daylight ebb.

A ship's chief sits where the cellarer sat and takes one sack in ten. He sells salt as fairly as the monks did and loot more cheaply. He asks whether the kings are still fighting each other, and is pleased with the answer.
Northmen are on the Garonne from 844 and the city is taken in 848. The wine still wants buyers; the sellers ask whether the salt island's new masters let a ship pass.
In July 846 the monastery burns. The lead that was not at Furca has run down the walls. Martinus has moved the lamp to the chapel by the old graves and lights it when there is fat.
No salt comes from the Loire this year. On the Seine a sack sells for two, and the man who has it is asked where he lay to load it.
The fish salters on the Canche pay double for bay salt and ask no questions of a boat that still brings it.
The canons have sent for the master of the boat that brought their book home. They have no bishop and no plate. They have a margin, and they have written in it.

endings.how: You took the clerk and the Bible off the lagoon side on the night ebb and carried them up the Loire.
endings.text: The book goes back on its desk in a cathedral that has no bishop. The canons write your house's name in its margin, small, by the Gospel for Saint John's day. Martinus is not suspected: you were never seen.
endings.reward: Sets bk_carried and herio_bible_home; a great deed in the Loire country; 300 pennies from the canons, paid over two years; sanctuary and free lodging at Namnetis; Martinus a fast friend.

endings.how: You sold bread and wine in Conca and bought church plate by weight.
endings.text: It is the cheapest silver you will ever buy and it cannot be sold in a Christian market without a story. The clerk is found at the next ebb. Martinus sells you salt afterwards and does not ask you into the hut.
endings.reward: Church plate worth about 500 pennies if it can be melted or carried north; a deed the church remembers against the house; the chief friendly; Martinus cool.

endings.how: You loaded salt on the lagoon side and sailed with the ebb, asking nothing.
endings.text: You are one of the few who still sail for salt, and salt is dear everywhere north of the Loire that year. You never learn what became of the clerk. The chronicle says he got away.
endings.reward: A hold of salt that sells at double in the Seine and the Rhine mouth while the Loire is shut; sets df_warned if the news of Nantes is carried to Rotomagus or Quentovic before Michaelmas.

stories.reward: The canons of Nantes in your debt, or a hold of cheap silver, or simply the salt when nobody else dares fetch it.

works.name: A lamp at the saint's head
works.what: Three lamps burn at the head of the marble coffin by day and by night. A layman may give the oil for one of them, year by year, and his name is said at the tomb.
works.picture: A hanging glass lamp on three chains with a small steady flame, white marble beneath it, a monk on a stool trimming the wick.
works.needs: Olive oil brought to the cellarer (four jars), or its price; alms given once at the tomb.
works.gives: Standing with the house and with every church on the Loire; act:heal at the tomb is free to your crew; the cellarer sells you salt before any other ship. It must be renewed each year with one jar of oil.
works.source: Ermentarius, Miracula II.8 (three lamps always lit); Vita Filiberti c. 27 (lamp oil from Bordeaux). The price is goods_793.json olive_oil

works.name: Bread for the windbound
works.what: In the founder's day ships held in the bay by foul winds were given beasts, flour and bread. A gift of corn to the guest house keeps the custom in a lean year.
works.picture: Seamen in rough cloaks sitting along a bench outside a gate, a monk handing round loaves from a basket, bare masts in the bay behind them.
works.needs: Thirty sacks' worth of corn or its price, given to the cellarer.
works.gives: act:lodge and act:provision are free for your own crew here while it lasts (three years); Breton and Bordeaux skippers met in the bay are friendly at first hail and pass on their news.
works.source: Vita Filiberti c. 29: windbound Breton ships given two beasts, flour and bread; the Rule of St Benedict c. 53

works.name: A salt bed of your own
works.what: A square of clay on the lagoon side with its bank, its sluice and a turf hut, cut and raked for your house by the islanders for a share.
works.picture: A shallow square of still water edged with white, a plank sluice, a turf hut with a rake against it, a woman drawing salt to the bank.
works.needs: The leave of whoever holds the shore: the cellarer to 836, the islanders' lord or the chief in Conca after; a raker to work it (Maura's people).
works.gives: Each autumn sixteen sacks of bay salt wait at the bed (works_793.json salt_pan). It can be lost to a storm flood, a raid or a lord's whim.
works.source: works_793.json salt_pan; laymen sell and give salt works at Guerande in Redon's charters (?). Beds on the island itself are supposed, not attested (Cartron 2010 ch. III)

works.name: A length of the abbot's wall
works.what: Abbot Hilbod is raising a rampart round the monastery with the abbey's own means. A merchant who pays for a length of bank and palisade is given a locked store inside it.
works.picture: Men with baskets of earth building a bank against a line of sharpened stakes, an abbot pointing with a rod, the church roof behind.
works.needs: Hilbod as abbot and at least easy with you; oak stakes or the silver for them.
works.gives: A store inside the fort (act:store without fee, safe from a raid while the fort stands); act:sanctuary for your crew; your goods are among those carried to the mainland when the monks leave in 836.
works.source: Diploma of Louis and Lothar, 2 August 830: the castrum built by Hilbod around the monastery between 824 and 830 (Poupardin 1905; Cartron 2010 ch. II). That laymen paid towards it is the game's (?)

works.name: Lead for the priory roof
works.what: The few monks sent from Tournus keep the founder's empty grave under a patched roof. Sheets of lead would close it against the rain for the first time since the burning.
works.picture: Two monks on a low roof laying grey sheets over old rafters, a third below holding a ladder, scorched stone still showing on the wall.
works.needs: Lead brought by sea (twelve loads) or its price; the prior's leave.
works.gives: Standing with Tournus and its houses up the Loire and the Saone; the prior keeps a berth and a bed for your house; Mass is said for your dead at the old tomb each twentieth of August.
works.source: A priory of Tournus about 1000 (fr.wikipedia Abbaye Saint-Philibert de Noirmoutier; the parish's page); the abbey's lead is Ermentarius, Miracula I.81. The church was rebuilt only in the late eleventh century; this roof is the game's (?)

ships.note: The islanders' own boats for the stake nets and the run to Furca. One is for sale when a fisherman drowns or grows old; Maura knows which.
ships.picture: A small open boat lying on her bilge on wet sand, a stone anchor beside her, nets drying over the gunwale.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json west_small_boat; islanders with boats are implied by Ermentarius, Miracula I.81 and II.9 (?)

ships.note: The abbey keeps sea boats to reach its mainland port and its salt works. The cellarer lets one with her steersman to a merchant he trusts, for a share of the freight.
ships.picture: A beamy open boat with one square sail running before the wind across a wide bay, a monk sitting amidships among sacks.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json coaster_minster_ship; the crossing to Furca before a north-west wind: Ermentarius, Miracula I.2

ships.note: Six boats of the abbey go free of toll on the Loire, the Allier, the Cher and the Dordogne. Space aboard one, with the abbey's man, carries a friend's goods upriver untolled.
ships.picture: A long low river boat under oars on a broad brown river, a monk in the stern holding up a sealed parchment to a man on a jetty.
ships.source: Diploma of Pippin I, 18 May 826, confirming a lost grant of Louis the Pious (Poupardin 1905)

sayings.text: Because of the ebbs our men cannot always reach the island. The Northmen can, whenever the sea is calm.
sayings.source: The king's council of 836 in Ermentarius, Miracula I.1 (Poupardin 1905), the dossier's rendering

sayings.text: They brought grain and took away only salt.
sayings.source: Ermentarius, Miracula I.81, of the Breton ships, the dossier's rendering

sayings.text: A measure of wine was a penny, unless I am mistaken.
sayings.source: Ermentarius, Miracula I.71, of the market at Deas about 838, the dossier's rendering

sayings.text: He swore by Saint Philibert that the halfpenny was his own, and the saint let him keep the halfpenny and took back the wine.
sayings.source: A joke made from Ermentarius, Miracula I.71: the man given his change by mistake, who came back to spend it and threw up what he drank

sayings.text: Steal the saint's bullock and you will row uphill until you bring it back.
sayings.source: A proverb made in the period's manner from Vita Filiberti c. 28: Breton sailors stole a bullock and the sea rose against them until they returned the hide and the meat

sayings.text: Count the birds before you count the spears.
sayings.source: Invented in the period's manner, after Ermentarius, Miracula II.10: a Saracen ship turned back because the shore was so thick with birds that they took them for an army

sayings.text: The monks leave with the swallows' coming and are back when the swallows go. The heathen keep the same calendar.
sayings.source: Invented in the period's manner; from 819 the monks spent early spring to the end of autumn at Deas (diploma of 2 August 830)

sayings.text: Let all guests who come be received as Christ.
sayings.source: The Rule of St Benedict c. 53, our rendering

easter_eggs.text: The hazel nut that ripens about the saint's feast on the twentieth day of August is called after him: the filbert.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia Philibert of Jumieges; the name is recorded much later (?)

easter_eggs.text: On the shore towards the north-west point three great stones stand with a fourth laid across them. The monks say giants; the islanders dry nets on it.
easter_eggs.source: The dolmen at L'Herbaudiere (fr.wikipedia Ile de Noirmoutier); what anybody said of it is the game's

easter_eggs.text: The island is Herio, and its monastery Herio monasterium. Say it fast for three hundred years and it becomes Hermoutier, then Noirmoutier; the 'black monastery' is a later guess at the sound.

A Breton crew that took the abbey's lead lay becalmed at Batz and saw a horseman with three spears charge them across the sea. A cripple there, cured in a dream, was sent to tell them why they had no wind.
A Breton fleet once landed at Conca to plunder and fell to killing one another on the sand. One man lived, and it was he who told the islanders.
A traveller's tale in Arabic, three lifetimes on, tells of an island off this coast twenty miles by three, with sweet wells, fine saffron and no snakes.
easter_eggs.source: A tenth-century Arabic notice read by its editor as Noirmoutier (fr.wikipedia Ile de Noirmoutier) (?)

easter_eggs.text: The stone coffins in the old graveyard are older than the monastery. Some have been borrowed twice.
easter_eggs.source: Le Vieil, a Gallo-Roman site reused as a Merovingian burial ground (Cartron 2010 ch. III)

easter_eggs.text: At the tomb the sick are given wine in which the saint's staff has been washed. The cellarer measures that wine as well.
easter_eggs.source: Ermentarius, Miracula I.2; the cellarer's measuring is the game's

unlocks.what: The cellarer's tally: salt on trust
unlocks.how: End the story herio.three_lamps by feeding the lamps, or bring corn or oil to the cellarer in three different years before 836.
unlocks.gives: A full hold of salt may be taken on a split tally stick and paid for on the next call (commission; the debt is kept as npc.cellarer.owed). Salt is offered to you before any other ship.

unlocks.what: A bench in the guest house
unlocks.how: Fund the work herio.work.windbound_dole or herio.work.lamp, or be friendly with any monk of the house.
unlocks.gives: act:lodge and act:provision cost nothing here; act:rumours gives the news of every ship windbound in the bay; a sick man of the crew may be left with the brothers (health).

unlocks.how: Hire Ursus on three calls, or be a fast friend of Ursus or Martinus.
unlocks.gives: Counts towards unlock_pilot_loire: no pilot's fee on this water, the grounding check on the bar passed as sure, and the day stick shows when the monastery's channel dries.

unlocks.what: A berth on the lagoon side
unlocks.how: End herio.three_lamps by selling on the sand, or herio.saints_road by standing with the island; or be a fast friend of Martinus.
unlocks.gives: From 836 the boat can lie unseen from Conca: a fleet in the bay does not find her (the raid card's check passes as likely), and salt is loaded at the islanders' own price whoever holds the island.

unlocks.how: End the story herio.emperors_cousin by carrying the letter and the book.
unlocks.gives: From 821 Corbie's agent at Quentovic buys from you first and lodges you free; Anskar and other pupils of Corbie in the north are friendly at first meeting (npc feeling); one letter of commendation to any abbey of the realm (show_charter, once).

unlocks.how: End the story herio.saints_road by carrying the saint to Furca.
unlocks.gives: Inherited by your heirs: lodging and a hearing wherever the saint's house then is, and goods carried untolled in the abbey's six boats on the Loire while they sail (toll).
